title: French Colony of Guiana
capsule: French Guiana has been a French colonial possession on the northeastern coast of South America since the seventeenth century, with Cayenne established as the colonial capital; the Wikidata window of 1791–1792 corresponds to the early Revolutionary period when the National Assembly reorganised colonial administration under the Constitution of 1791. The colony's economy rested on plantation agriculture dependent on enslaved African labour, and the 1794 abolition decree—though unevenly enforced—generated significant upheaval before Napoleon restored slavery in 1802. The territory passed briefly to Portuguese control from 1809–1817 following the Napoleonic Wars before the Congress of Vienna restored it to France, and it became infamous as a penal colony (including Devil's Island) from 1852 until 1953 before being reorganised as an overseas department in 1946.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. French Guiana's colonial-era boundaries were contested with Dutch and Portuguese neighbours throughout the early modern period; the western boundary with Suriname (Maroni River) and the southern interior limits were formally delimited only in the nineteenth century and by a 1900 Swiss arbitration with Brazil.
